- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are flat or rising slowly, expect overshoot or overconfidence; correct by reducing slope or adding downward bias.
- If sentiment turns bearish (≤0.33) after a spike, model often fails to adjust quickly — apply mean reversion or downward correction with lag penalty.
- High event count (≥15 events/30d) with net supply negative and bearish sentiment → model tends to overestimate recovery; reduce forecast by 5–10% relative to prior period.
- After a sharp spike (e.g., >10% from prior), model often overcorrects downward — apply “overshoot correction” by adding 1–2% upward bias to offset lag.
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and event balance is neutral, model tends to drift toward prior mean — apply “sentiment-weighted mean reversion” to anchor forecast near recent sentiment-weighted average.
- If model forecast is flat (±0.1) over 5+ days with no event change, check for sentiment drift — if sentiment turns bearish, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5 units per day.
- For high event density (≥18 events/30d) with net supply negative, model often underestimates volatility — increase forecast variance or add 1–2% downward bias to reflect bearish sentiment.
